lesson.title: Blood on the Monongahela: The Homestead Strike of 1892
lesson.summary: In the summer of 1892, a wage dispute at Andrew Carnegie's Homestead steel plant erupted into an armed battle between striking workers and private Pinkerton guards, dealing organized labor in the steel industry a defeat it would not recover from for decades.
lesson.body:
The Homestead Works, located along the Monongahela River near Pittsburgh, was one of the largest and most modern steel plants in the world and a centerpiece of Andrew Carnegie's steel empire. Skilled workers there belonged to the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers, a craft union representing skilled steelworkers, part of the same broad era of trade union organizing as the Knights of Labor, though by 1892 it functioned more like the narrower trade unions the AFL represented, focused on skilled workers rather than the whole plant workforce.

In the summer of 1892, with Carnegie away in Scotland, plant manager Henry Clay Frick, a fierce opponent of organized labor, proposed steep wage cuts when the union's contract came up for renewal. When the union refused to accept the cuts, Frick locked the workers out and began preparing to bring in strikebreakers to reopen the plant.

On July 6, 1892, Frick hired roughly 300 armed Pinkerton detectives and attempted to bring them up the river by barge to seize the plant. Striking workers and Homestead townspeople met them at the riverbank, and a gun battle broke out that left several men dead on both sides before the Pinkertons surrendered and were driven out of town. The strikers had won the battle, but not the strike.

Pennsylvania's governor, Robert Pattison, responded by sending roughly 8,000 state militia troops to occupy Homestead and protect the strikebreakers Frick brought in to reopen the plant. Public sympathy for the strikers, already strained by the violence, was damaged further later that month when an anarchist named Alexander Berkman, who had no real connection to the union, attempted to assassinate Frick. The attack let Frick and other employers paint the strikers as dangerous radicals, even though the union itself had not been involved.

The strike collapsed by November 1892, and the union at Homestead was effectively destroyed. Steelworkers would not successfully organize again on a large scale until the 1930s, during the New Deal era. The defeat showed how far industrialists were willing to go to break a union, and how readily state power sided with employers when labor conflict turned violent, a pattern that would repeat two years later on an even larger scale in the Pullman Strike.
